Whisk research is done. Here's what matters:

Whisk was a free Google Labs experiment (launched Dec 16, 2024, US-only at first) that let you "prompt with images" instead of text. You'd drop in three roles: a subject image, a scene image, a style image (later up to 8 references), optionally add text, and hit generate. The unusual part is the pipeline: Gemini first wrote a detailed caption of each input image, then fed those descriptions into Imagen 3 (Imagen 4 from May 2025). And the auto-written caption was inspectable and editable — a hidden notepad you could click into, rewrite, and regenerate. Every submit returned images in pairs, with refine (full regeneration), an animate option via Veo 2, and shareable "recipe" links others could remix.

Now why the images look the way they do — this is the big one: every remix went through the lossy image→caption→image bottleneck. Identity survived only as Gemini's prose, so re-generating the "same" subject produced same-face drift, changing height, weight, hairstyle, skin tone (Google warned about this explicitly). Caption hallucinations became prompt ground truth, which is where anatomy artifacts come from. Long or multi-reference prompts diluted elements, dropping or fusing figures. Dice presets, templates (sticker, plushie, enamel pin), and pair outputs produced repetitive motif families, and refine regenerated whole images, so you'd get drifting near-duplicate clusters — those same-second bursts of 8-14 near-identical gens you saw are exactly this. Opaque policy blocks and silently-completed background generations explain the sequence gaps. Also: free, unlimited-ish, no credits — that's what made 9,868 images possible at all.

One caveat: Whisk was reportedly retired April 30, 2026, folded into Google Flow — but I couldn't find an official Google announcement, only secondary sources. Also couldn't verify exact output resolution or any hard daily cap.
